name: Estrogen topical for hair
lead: Topical estrogen for hair refers to estrogenic solutions applied to the scalp for pattern hair loss, with the aim of keeping more of the hair a person has so the hairline and crown look fuller for longer. The best-documented example is alfatradiol (17-alpha-estradiol), a weak estrogen and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold as an ethanol-based scalp solution in Germany and several Latin American countries under names such as Ell-Cranell Alpha, Avicis, Avixis and Pantostin.[1]

Wikipedia describes alfatradiol as used continuously for pattern hair loss in men and women, with limited regrowth of lost hair and poorer response in advanced alopecia.[1] A 1980 randomized double-blind study reported reduced androgenic hair loss without effective new growth, and a 2007 university-led study of 103 women found minoxidil performed better than alfatradiol, which slowed or stabilized loss without increasing hair density or thickness.[1]

Estrogen is also associated with thicker hair during pregnancy, and estradiol has documented skin effects, but its role as a hair-loss treatment beyond alfatradiol is not established in general medical references.[2][3]

paras: Alfatradiol is a stereoisomer of 17-beta-estradiol, differing only in the stereochemistry at carbon 17. It binds estrogen receptors with much lower activity, and is described as having roughly 100-fold lower estrogenic activity, and it inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.[1] Dihydrotestosterone is the hormone implicated in androgenetic hair loss.[2]

Alfatradiol is applied to the scalp as an ethanolic solution and must be used continuously to keep preventing further hair loss, according to Wikipedia; regrowth of lost hair is limited, and advanced alopecia generally responds poorly to treatment.[1] For comparison, Wikipedia's androgenetic alopecia article describes minoxidil as the best-supported treatment for female pattern hair loss.[4]

Local burning or itching, attributed to the ethanol vehicle, and increased sebum production are reported for alfatradiol; its leaflet advises against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under age 18 [1]. Estradiol more broadly is associated with clotting and hormone-sensitive cancer risks in general discussions, though these are described for estrogen use overall rather than topical scalp products specifically [3].
Alfatradiol has also been studied for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, and a 2017 mouse study reported improved insulin resistance and metabolic function without feminisation.[1]

A 1980 randomized, double-blind study of alfatradiol (Orfanos and Vogels) reported no systemic side effects and a reduction in androgenic hair loss, but no effective new hair growth.[1] A 2007 university-led study of 103 women (Blume-Peytavi et al.) compared it with minoxidil: minoxidil performed better, while alfatradiol slowed or stabilised hair loss without increasing density or thickness.[1] No studies were found of topical 17-beta-estradiol or other estrogen preparations specifically for hair loss.

card.summary: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol, that may slow thinning in some regions but are not shown to regrow hair.
card.note: Not widely approved; label advises against use in pregnancy and under 18.

quick.overview:
Topical estrogen for hair usually means alfatradiol, a weak estrogen scalp solution sold in some countries for pattern hair loss.

Reports describe it slowing or stabilizing loss rather than thickening hair, and minoxidil outperformed it in a women's study.
quick.mechanism: Alfatradiol binds estrogen receptors weakly and inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of testosterone to DHT.
quick.risks: Scalp irritation from the alcohol vehicle and more oil production are reported. Safety in pregnancy and minors is unknown.

chain: Weak estrogen solution applied to the scalp
Hair loss slowed or stabilised, so more existing hair is kept
angle.text: Alfatradiol is applied to the scalp to slow androgen-driven thinning, so existing hair is retained rather than lost. In the studies described, it stabilised loss more than it thickened hair.
